questions.prompt: Which part of the bulb glows to make light?
questions.explanation: The filament is the deliberately thin wire that heats up and glows.
questions.misconception: The glass only lets light out; the heat is all in the filament.

questions.prompt: Why does the filament get hot?
options: Current meets resistance as it squeezes through
questions.explanation: The thin filament resists the current, turning some moving energy into heat — and heat makes it glow.
questions.misconception: The bulb's warmth is often blamed on the outside; it is made inside by resistance.

questions.prompt: You open the switch in the bulb's loop. What happens?
options: It keeps glowing dimly for a while
questions.explanation: Current needs a complete loop; a break anywhere stops it and the bulb goes dark at once.
questions.misconception: The idea that stored heat keeps the bulb lit; without current the glow is instant-off.

questions.prompt: Old light bulbs are warm when on. Why?
options: Most of the energy becomes heat, not light
The glass makes heat by itself
Light turns to heat on the glass
questions.explanation: Incandescent bulbs waste most input as heat; only a few percent becomes visible light.
questions.misconception: Assuming all energy becomes light; heat is the biggest side effect, which is why LEDs win.

questions.prompt: More current through the same filament means the bulb...
questions.explanation: More current = hotter filament = brighter light — the bulb's brightness follows the flow.
questions.misconception: Some invert the relation; more flow always means a hotter, brighter coil.
